the shift to a progestin is associated with a high level of satisfaction in the majority of women with persistent pain after treatment with estrogen-progestin oral contraceptives for endometriotic disease.
70% of women with endometriosis were very satisfied or satisfi ed with NETA treatment and the majority (58/125, 47%) experienced suboptimal tolerability.
70% of women with endometriosis who were dissatisfied with the treatment with low-dose OC and had moderate to severe pain symptoms were satisfied with the oral NETA treatment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a shift to a progestin when estrogens-progestins are inefficacious for endometriasis-associated pain.
the efficacy of a progestin in women with symptomatic disease not responding to OC.
the evaluation of a new treatment option in women with endometriosis-associated pain not responding to oral contraceptive treatment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of a progestin in women with endometriosis who have not responded to an estrogen-progestin combination is a worthwhile option.
oral NET-A is a valid alternative for women with symptomatic disease not responding to OC, but it is not a panacea and its efficacy should be evaluated in a randomized trial against placebo.
the shift to oral NETA from OC in women with endometriosis-associated pain is worthwhile, but not in all cases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NETA is an effective alternative to OC for endometriotic women with persistence of pain symptoms.
shifting to oral progestin is a good choice for women who have persistent pain symptoms while taking OCs.
the use of NETA as a first-line therapy for endometriomas is effective and has a high level of patient satisfaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
oral progestins can provide a safe and effective option to treat women with endometriosis who are not responding to estrogen–progestins.
NETA is effective and well tolerated for the treatment of endometriosis-associated pain in a large proportion of patients who are dissatisfied with OC.
a shift from an estrogen–progestin to a progestin is worthwhile when estrogen–progestins have been inefficacious for endometrioma pain.
